_comment: Task recipes — the written half of the user guide. The other half
(docs/REFERENCE.md) is generated from the code and never edited by hand.
Every step names a real route and a string that must actually render on it.
scripts/check-guide-drift.mjs verifies both: routes against the generated
reference (cheap, runs anywhere) and the on-screen text against the running
app (inside the local-stack harness). A renamed button therefore breaks the
build instead of quietly making the guide lie to a new user.
Written as TASKS, not as features. Nobody opens a manual wanting to read
about the Work Orders Module; they want to file one and get back to work.
audience: Building superintendents, porters and property managers. Assumes no software background — assumes you know the building.

tasks.title: Sign in for the first time
tasks.why: Everything else needs you signed in. Your account is created by whoever runs your company's SupersDeck — you cannot sign yourself up, which is deliberate: it keeps your buildings' data closed to everyone outside your organisation.

steps.do: Open the app. You land on the sign-in screen.
Enter the email address your manager used to invite you, and your password.
You arrive at the dashboard, which greets you by time of day and shows what needs attention.

tasks.title: File a work order
tasks.why: The core of the day. A resident calls about no heat, a light is out, a door will not latch — this is how it gets recorded, assigned and closed, with a record you can show later.

steps.do: From the dashboard, open the pending list to see everything currently outstanding.
Create a new work order. Give it the building, a short title describing the problem, and a priority.
Back on the dashboard the new ticket appears in the day's list.

tasks.title: Log a heat and hot-water reading
tasks.why: During heat season New York City requires indoor and outdoor readings. Logging them here builds the record that answers an HPD complaint before it becomes a violation.

steps.do: Open the heat log entry form.
Pick the building, then enter the indoor and outdoor temperatures you measured.
Check the compliance view to see the readings against what the city requires.

tasks.title: Add a building
tasks.why: Done once per property, usually at setup. Everything else — work orders, heat logs, units, tenants — hangs off a building, so this comes first.

steps.do: Open the buildings list to see what is already set up.
Add a new building with its address, borough, and the number of units and floors.

tasks.title: Invite someone to your team
tasks.why: New porter, new super, a manager who needs visibility. Only an admin can do this, and the role you choose decides what they can reach — see the permission groups in REFERENCE.md.

steps.do: Open your team roster. You see everyone in your organisation.
Invite the new person by email and choose their role: porter, super, manager or admin.

tasks.title: Record a contractor's visit
tasks.why: Who was in the building, when, and for what. This is the log you reach for after an incident, and it is what an insurer or a board asks to see.

steps.do: Open the on-site logbook to see recent visits.
Contractors can also sign themselves in by scanning the QR poster at the door — print one per building.

tasks.title: See where you stand on compliance
tasks.why: The view a manager or board member asks about. What is open, what is due, and what has already been handled.
